rows.what: John Anderson Wear, buried at West Park — who is he?
rows.note: STRUCK within the hour, and it is worth saying why. The Find a Grave record's PLACE field offers five candidate cemeteries for the ambiguous string 'West Park Cemetery' — Johannesburg, Cleveland Ohio, Long Eaton Derbyshire, Hereford Texas, and Bulawayo — and FamilySearch surfaced the Johannesburg one only because the query was filtered to South Africa. The record's own Country, State, County and City fields resolve to UNITED STATES OF AMERICA / TEXAS / DEAF SMITH / HEREFORD. He also appears as a father in Illinois births of 1883. He is an American and has nothing to do with this family. A place-name collision in an index, caught before anything was published — which is the first time this week that has happened before rather than after.

rows.what: 64 Greenfield Road, Greenside — find out who lived there
rows.note: DONE 15 September — overtaken rather than answered, and the detour was worth more than the row. The gazette gives nothing for 64 Greenfield Road, so instead of hunting the address the CEMETERY REGISTERS were opened, on the reasoning that a burial register records where the dead lived and a grave register records who BOUGHT the grave. Both are true. West Park Cemetery Private Graves Register, folio W 8 (published here first as W58; corrected the same evening): purchaser WEAR, Mr L. A. R., of 271 WILSON STREET, FAIRLANDS, receipt 11484, 13 September 1969, sixty pounds, grave 56045 section E.C., person buried HENRY ROBERT WEAR. Read at five times magnification the initial is a cursive L, not a J. And the 1986 burial register gives Martha Maud, aged 90, died at the Hillcrest Geriatric Centre, usual residence 12 and a half Second Street, PARKHURST — buried in grave 56045, the same grave. Row 55's own question is still unanswered; it has been overtaken, because the archive now has an address for LEONARD, which is what it actually wanted.

rows.what: Henrique’s Portuguese military record — now at the Arquivo Geral do Exército
rows.owner: the Arquivo Geral do Exército, Lisboa
rows.note: A reply came in at 06:54 on 15 September and was sitting unread. Maria Joao Pires, Coordinator of the Arquivo da Defesa Nacional, writes that for military records one must contact the ARQUIVO GERAL DO EXERCITO, arqgex@exercito.pt — a different body from the Arquivo Historico Militar this archive had already written to. Written to the same hour, citing the referral by name and date, Gmail 1a0a40447162eada. The prize is the same as it always was: a Portuguese military recenseamento names the father AND the mother of the man recensed, and Henrique's father is unknown. Row 33 makes this more important, not less — the South African civil registers have no parentage field at all, so the Portuguese paperwork is the only route left for him. Acknowledged the same day at 07:42: "Confirma-se a receção da sua correspondência eletrónica a qual será tratada pelos nossos serviços." So the referral address works. An acknowledgement, not an answer.

rows.what: Who authorised the second burial in grave 56045 in 1986
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the answer is that THE RECORD WAS NEVER MADE. Four more West Park images were rebuilt tile by tile. (1) The full two-page spread of Martha Maud's 1986 burial, folio W 104, image 3:1:3QHV-B3PY-2FKN, 7,407 x 3,164, 377 tiles: cause NATURAL CAUSES, burial order 37640, 17.3.86, undertaker REG, receipt 61610, R70.00, nature of interment "New Reopen." — and the Remarks column, which is where an authority would be noted, is EMPTY for her row. Not illegible, not cropped: empty. (2) The index side of the Private Graves folio, image 3:1:3QHV-13P1-89VT, read line by line across three magnified passes, holds exactly ONE Wear: Henry Robert, 13.9.69, grave 5604/5, Fol. W56. MARTHA MAUD IS NOT IN IT. A 1986 interment into a 1969 private grave generated no new private-grave entry, which is itself the explanation for the blank Remarks column: the reopening was handled as a burial, not as a grave transaction, so nobody had to sign for it. The row closes with the reason attached, not struck. What is left is the undertaker's own file — the register names REG — or Martha Maud's estate at the Master of the High Court, and neither is worth a row until the Master answers what it already has. THE DETOUR PAID AGAIN, twice: burial register folio W 56 row 4 gives HENRY ROBERT WEAR's usual residence, 5 LIVINGSTONE CT., 4TH ST., PARKHURST — the first address ever recorded for him in South Africa — with address at time of death General Hospital Jhb., died 11.9.69 of BRONCHOPNEUMONIA aged 80, burial order 2894, undertaker Cooks, R15.00. And the folio number this archive published for the grave register was WRONG: it is W 8, not W58, confirmed three ways.

rows.what: 5 Livingstone Court, 4th Street, Parkhurst — run the parents' documented address
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and it paid far beyond the address. One gazette query on "Livingstone Court" returned four South African hits; the 1965 and 1977 ones are other people, but GOVERNMENT GAZETTE 4620 OF 21 MARCH 1975, under NATURALIZATION NOTICES, carries: EVANS, Mrs Janette Eileen Maud, formerly Bailey, nee WEAR, saleslady, 5 LIVINGSTONE COURT, 28 VIERDE STRAAT/FOURTH STREET, PARKHURST, JOHANNESBURG. The OCR interleaves two columns and the entry had to be unpicked from its neighbour, so the page itself was read. And the grant followed in GAZETTE 5007 OF 12 MARCH 1976: R54033 - EVANS, Janette Eileen Maud, 28/10/19, England, Citizen of the U.K. and C., 30/10/75. THREE GAINS. (1) The Parkhurst address is corroborated from a wholly independent source six years later, with the building's street number added — the cemetery clerk's hand and the Government Printer's type agree. (2) The birth date 28 October 1919 falls inside GRO quarter Q4 1919, so the Hitchin birth and the Johannesburg naturalisation are the same woman without an assumption. (3) THE FAMILY STAYED BRITISH: Leonard's eldest sister was still a citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies in 1975, forty years after the household left Hertfordshire. That explains why a man in Johannesburg from the late 1930s to 1969 leaves so little in South African government series. Also new: she was married twice, formerly BAILEY. Checked and rejected along the way: "Wear, Martha" in Gazette 2438 of 20 June 1969 is MARTHA CUMMINGS WEAR, BORN CAMASK, of 17 Botha Avenue, Witbank, estate 6167/66 — not Martha Maud born Castle. Opened rather than trusted, which is now the rule.

rows.what: 271 Wilson Street, Fairlands — establish whether Leonard owned or rented it
rows.note: NEW, and it follows from the parents being at a DIFFERENT address on the same day. On 13 September 1969 Henry Robert Wear's household was a Parkhurst flat and L. A. R. Wear's was 271 Wilson Street, Fairlands. So the Fairlands address is Leonard's own, not a borrowed family one — which makes it worth testing in a way a family address would not be. A Deeds Office search on the erf will say whether he held title, and if he did it will say when he bought and WHEN HE SOLD OR DIED OUT OF IT, which bears directly on 1973 against 1979. Costs a search fee and needs somebody in Johannesburg; add to the held researcher brief rather than opening a correspondence. || REASSIGNED 16 September: this was never a desk job and should not have sat under "this archive". A Deeds Office search on the erf needs a person in Johannesburg. It belongs with REQUEST 14's Deeds Registry question, which already asks about the ante-nuptial contracts, rather than standing alone.

rows.what: Folio F 3/8 — the possible transfer of the grave rights
rows.note: NEW and deliberately small. Row 4 of burial folio W 56 carries two lines in its Remarks column: "P. Fol. W.8.", which is the private-graves cross-reference and is certainly Wear's, and above it, in a smaller darker hand, "Transf. P.Fol. F 3/8." — a transfer of private rights to or from folio F 3/8. The ruling below both lines puts them in row 4's cell, but the page curves across two thousand pixels and the upper line may belong to row 3. THE ARCHIVE IS NOT CLAIMING IT. If it does belong to Wear then the grave rights in 56045 were transferred, and whoever they were transferred to is a name this archive does not have — which is the question row 57 asked and could not answer from the books it opened. Resolving it means finding the F-series folio in the same film and reading what grave it covers. One image, no fee. 15 September, partly answered without opening the F folio: the Private Graves Register HAS an "Authority to Purchase — Next of Kin" column and IT IS BLANK, for Wear and for six consecutive neighbouring rows (receipts 10997, 10999, 11009, 11475, 11484, 11517). The clerk on folio W 8 never used that column. So even had the 1986 reopening been recorded, the register's relationship field was not being filled in. The F 3/8 folio is still worth one image, but it is now the only thing this book can still give. || BLOCKED 16 September: THE FAMILYSEARCH SESSION HAS SIGNED OUT and this row cannot move without it. The catalogue and persona APIs now return 401 and the site redirects to the login page. This archive will not enter credentials on David's behalf. One sign-in in the browser unblocks this row, rows 42, 60 and 88 together, and the post-1970 marriage register test in row 81. *** UNBLOCKED 17 SEPTEMBER: the sign-in is live, and the row now has its image references. *** The West Park pages are ark 3:1:3QHK-Q3PY-2FQG and 3:1:3QHV-13PY-2FCC for Henry Robert in 1969, and 3:1:3QHV-B3PY-2FKN for Martha Maud in 1986, all in Johannesburg Cemetery Records, collection 4453927. Written into data/familysearch-sa-family.tsv so the next attempt starts inside the film rather than looking for it. What still has to be done by eye is finding the F-series folio in the same film and reading what grave it covers. NOT DONE TODAY, and said plainly rather than left looking done. || BLOCKED AGAIN 20 SEPTEMBER: THE FAMILYSEARCH SESSION HAS SIGNED OUT for the second time in four days. The search page now says 'Create a free account or sign in to see all available results' and the persona API returns 0 results for a query that returned 111 on 17 September — a zero that means signed out, not absent, which is exactly the kind of false negative this archive keeps catching. I do not sign anybody in. One sign-in in the browser unblocks this row and row 174 together. || 20 SEPTEMBER: THE SIGN-IN IS BACK AND THIS ROW WAS STILL NOT DONE, which is said plainly rather than left implied. The session was spent on the Ermland parish registers instead, because Lizzy's birthplace surfaced the same morning and was the larger prize. The image references captured on 17 September stand and the row is ready: the F-series folio has to be found by eye in the same film as ark 3:1:3QHK-Q3PY-2FQG. NOT A NEW BLOCK — A CHOICE, AND THE ROW SHOULD NOT PRETEND OTHERWISE. *** AND THEN IT WAS ATTEMPTED AFTER ALL, AND GOT MOST OF THE WAY. *** The row has never named the film it needs. IT NOW DOES: the catalogue record behind the indexed collection is olib:4148464, 'South Africa, Johannesburg City Cemetery records', TWO HUNDRED AND TEN FILMS, twelve of them West Park private graves registers by year range. LEONARD BOUGHT GRAVE 56045 ON 13 SEPTEMBER 1969, SO FOLIO W 8 IS IN FILM 107638608, 'WPC PRIVATE GRAVES REGISTERS 1963-1970', 488 IMAGES — and nowhere else. The film was opened and its structure read off the page: IT IS ALPHABETICAL BY PURCHASER SURNAME, image 401 is the T section (Theunissen, Tyson, Terblanche, Tennyson, Taljaard, Tomlinson, Taylor), the printed form is 14/6082 and the columns are NAME OF PURCHASER and ADDRESS. So THE F FOLIOS SHOULD SIT AROUND IMAGES 180 TO 200 and the W folios around 440 to 470. FOLIO F 3/8 WAS NOT READ: the image viewer kept reverting to its thumbnail grid, each page load costs fifteen to twenty seconds, and the hunt was abandoned rather than padded out. THAT IS A FAIR TRADE AND THE ROW SAYS SO: the transfer line may not be Wear's at all — the ruling puts it in row 4's cell but the page curves and it may belong to row 3 — and a film number plus an alphabetical structure is worth more than another hour of clicking, because it makes every future West Park question cheap. In data/westpark-films.tsv.

rows.what: Naturalisation file R54033, and whether Leonard ever had one
rows.note: NEW, and it is a record class this archive has never used. A gazette naturalisation notice is a name and an address; the FILE behind it records date and place of birth, previous nationality and PARENTS. Row 33 established that the South African civil marriage registers have no parentage field at all — this series does. Certificate R54033 was granted to Janette Eileen Maud Evans, nee Wear, on 30 October 1975; if the file names Henry Robert Wear and Martha Maud Castle it is the first South African government record to state that couple as the parents of a child. It does not prove Leonard was theirs. THE SECOND QUESTION IS THE BIGGER ONE: ask in the same letter whether any naturalisation file exists for WEAR, Leonard Aubrey Robert, born 1917. A phrase search of the gazette returns nothing for him and no Wear in either the 1975 notice list or the 1976 grant list, but the lists are alphabetical and the OCR interleaves columns badly enough that this very entry had to be unpicked by hand — SO THAT NULL IS NOT AN ANSWER. Files for this period sit with the Department of Home Affairs, older series transferred to the National Archives, Pretoria. A letter, not a purchase. Send with the Master of the High Court business. || WORKED 16 September to the point of deciding WHO to ask, and the answer is nobody new. NAAIRS does not index individual naturalisation files — its 342 NATURALIZATION documents are policy files and bills — so the file behind certificate R54033 sits with the Department of Home Affairs or in an unindexed National Archives series. THE ARCHIVE ALREADY HAS TWO LIVE THREADS THAT COULD CARRY THE QUESTION: Enquiries2@dsac.gov.za, which answered within two days on 12-14 September, and Ms Mavis Xaba at mavisx@dsac.gov.za, WHO HAS ALREADY BEEN WRITTEN TO TWICE AND MUST NOT GET A THIRD COLD THREAD. So this is not a new letter: it is one added question on the existing NARS thread, asking whether naturalisation files of the 1970s are held by them or by Home Affairs, and whether the file behind a known certificate number can be produced. Cheap, and it avoids the duplication this archive has already been burned by once.

rows.what: The Bailey marriage — Janette Wear married twice
rows.note: DONE 16 September, AND IT IS THE BEST THING FOUND THIS WEEK. The archive did not know which country the Bailey marriage was in, let alone which year. It is the FIRST of the thirty-six, and it is ENGLAND. FreeBMD, Marriages, December quarter 1939, >99% complete: WEAR, Jeanette E M — spouse BAILEY — HITCHIN — vol 3a page 4416; and the reverse, BAILEY, EDWARD J — spouse WEAR — same volume and page. HITCHIN IS THE FAMILY'S OWN REGISTRATION DISTRICT, where all six Wear children were born. TWO CONSEQUENCES. First, it rewrites the 1939 Register. That register, taken 29 SEPTEMBER 1939, found her alone at 18 Ridge Avenue, Letchworth, and this archive read it as "and one daughter stayed" — the household gone to South Africa, a girl of twenty left behind. SHE WAS NOT LEFT BEHIND; SHE WAS STAYING TO BE MARRIED, within three months and probably less. Second, and this is the point: AN ENGLISH MARRIAGE CERTIFICATE NAMES BOTH FATHERS. Row 33 established that the South African register has no parents' column at all — which is why the whole sibship rests on a seven-person family tree, why request 19 goes to the Master for three estates, and why row 61 chases a naturalisation file. This certificate costs about £14 and comes by email.

rows.what: WLD 978/1960 — who was Mawthane Dabeah Kwele, and why was he suing Leonard
rows.note: NEW, and it is a fifth court file and a year the archive did not have. TAB, WLD 978/1960: ILLIQUID CASE, PAYMENT, MAWTHANE DABEAH KWELE VERSUS L A R WEAR. Leonard was in Johannesburg in 1960 and somebody sued him for money. The plaintiff's name is African, and a Black plaintiff bringing a payment action against a white defendant in the Witwatersrand Local Division in 1960 implies a working or trading relationship rather than a casual one — which would make this the only surviving trace of what Leonard actually DID for a living between the 1951 register's ENGINEER and the 1969 grave. The archive is not guessing further; the file would say. Add to the held researcher brief alongside the ante-nuptial contracts, since it is the same reading room. || FOLDED into REQUEST 20 on 16 September — the consolidated Pretoria court-file bundle. Between 15 and 16 September this archive found EIGHT files in one depot, from five separate lines of enquiry, opened as five separate rows. That is how research happens and a terrible way to commission it: one person, one visit, one list, in priority order so it can be cut from the bottom. The bundle is HELD, not sent — the researcher was engaged on 14 September for six Booyzen files and has not replied, and nothing more goes to her until she answers on rates and capacity. This row stays open only as a pointer to request 20.

rows.what: WLD 2961/1962 — the co-respondent named one number after the divorce
rows.note: NEW. WLD 2960/1962 is Marjorie Eileen Wear divorcing Leonard; WLD 2961/1962, filed one number later, is the same plaintiff suing ANOTHER WOMAN for DAMAGES. Same plaintiff, consecutive numbers, same year: in the practice of the period that is an action against the co-respondent, and it means the second marriage ended over somebody the archive has never heard of. HER NAME IS IN THE INDEX AND DELIBERATELY NOT ON THE SITE — she would be in her eighties or nineties if living, there is no death record for her, and the claim is an imputation of adultery drawn from two case numbers rather than from the file. Held in the private notes. What would settle it is the file itself, and it matters beyond gossip: a woman Leonard was involved with in 1962 is the likeliest person to have been near him in 1969, and 1969 is where he disappears. || FOLDED into REQUEST 20 on 16 September — the consolidated Pretoria court-file bundle. rows.what: Ivone's naturalisation — the one route that names her parents on a South African form
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the answer is a bounded negative that is itself a fact about her. The gazette was swept YEAR BY YEAR 1946-1980 for the forename Ivone — the search API takes a year filter and pages, which is how a common forename becomes tractable. Ten South African gazettes carry it in that window and EVERY ONE WAS OPENED: a Radium Station general dealer in 1951, Ivone da Conceicao Isaac in the 1962 grant list, Maria Ivone Freitas Basilio de Abreu of Emmarentia in 1967, Ivone Bertholet de Oliveira e Sousa Duran of Lourenco Marques in 1968, Maria Ivone Silva Almeida in the 1968 grant list, Maria Ivone Melo Gouveia in the 1970 list. NONE IS HER. The exact forms "Salkow, Ivone", "Ivone Salkow", "LUWINSKI, Ivone", "MOTA FIGUEIREDO" and "Rocha, Ivone" return zero each. IVONE DID NOT NATURALISE AS A SOUTH AFRICAN under any of her three surnames. The sweep also taught the format — surname, forenames, date of birth, country of birth, previous nationality, certificate number — and showed the lists FULL of Portuguese and Madeiran names through exactly the years she lived there. Other Portuguese naturalised steadily; she did not. That fits a woman who went back to Portugal and died at Porto, and it makes the Portuguese correspondence more important, not less.

rows.what: Da Rocha naturalisation — the father the family tree can only call Unknown
rows.note: DONE 15 September. "da Rocha, Henrique" and "Henrique Figueiredo Pinto" return three South African gazettes and ALL THREE ARE THE 2023 ESTATE NOTICES THIS ARCHIVE ALREADY HAD for estate 12294/2023. No naturalisation notice, no grant. The route is closed and the father the tree calls Unknown is still unknown. What remains for him is the Portuguese military recenseamento, which is row 56, and the South African estate file itself.

rows.what: Salkow's naturalisation, and whether he was an immigrant at all
rows.note: DONE 15 September. "Salkow, Morris", "Morris Isaac Salkow" and "Salkow, Mrs" all return zero. The bare surname returns scores of hits across 1941-1969 but they are trade and business notices, not persons. No naturalisation for him either. Where Morris Isaac Salkow was born is still unestablished, and the gazette will not say.

rows.what: Cynthia Halsey's estate — a death notice naming Henry Robert Wear and Martha Maud Castle
rows.note: WORKED 16 September to the point where only a letter remains, and the letter is written. REQUEST 19 IS DRAFTED AND NOT SENT, because this archive's own rule after the Xaba duplication is to verify the address before writing: the Johannesburg Master's office has not been checked the way Cape Town's was for request 11. THE ROW ALSO GAINED A THIRD SISTER. Cynthia Yvonne Elizabeth Halsey, born Wear, b.1931, DIED 2000 — the death was not previously fixed. And KATHLEEN EDITH FOOT, born Wear, b.1921, DIED 2010, married James Cecil Foot in 1945, is flagged in the ESTATE FILE index as well as the death index, which makes her the likeliest of the three to have a file that survives. CHECKED SO THE LETTER DOES NOT ASK WHAT THE SENDER COULD FIND: none of the three has a Government Gazette estate notice — "CYNTHIA YVONNE ELIZABETH" returns nothing at all, "JANETTE EILEEN MAUD" returns only her 1975 naturalisation, "KATHLEEN EDITH" with FOOT returns nothing in 2009-2014. That is expected rather than suspicious: a J193 advertisement is required only above a value threshold. So they must be asked for by name and date of death, which is what request 19 does. || ADDRESS CHECKED 16 September, and the check changed the letter. MastersJohannesburg@justice.gov.za is NOT IN USE — the department's own PDF says so in capitals. rows.what: Martha Maud Wear's 1986 estate — outside the index, so it must be asked for
rows.note: Row 36 established that the NAAIRS deceased-estate index STOPS AT THE END OF 1976, so the absence of a 1986 estate proves nothing: it is out of range, not missing. Martha Maud Wear died 16 March 1986 aged 90, usual residence 12½ Second Street, Parkhurst, and was buried in her husband's grave. Her estate would be at the Master of the High Court, Johannesburg. Its death notice names HER parents — the Castle side — and its next-of-kin and heirs schedule lists her surviving children, WHICH IS THE LIST THIS ARCHIVE MOST WANTS. If Leonard predeceased her the schedule normally says so and often gives the date. Fold into the Master correspondence already running as row 2.

rows.what: The England and Wales probate calendar, 1970–1990, for Leonard
rows.note: WORKED 15 September to the end of what is free, and the result is a second instrument on which 1973 fails. The England and Wales probate service is free and its images ARE viewable without an account — but IT DOES NOT NAME-INDEX ANYTHING BEFORE 1996. A surname-and-year search returns scanned calendar pages and matches the string anywhere on the page, so WEAR also catches Weardale and Wearmouth. Searched with the keyword AUBREY to cut the noise: 1973 returns ZERO PAGES; then 8, 24, 19, 31, 13, 23, 19, 13 for 1974 to 1981. THE FAMILY TREE'S YEAR RETURNS NOTHING, on a second independent index, the evening after the South African estate index said the same. The 1979 pages have NOT been read — twenty-three dense calendar pages is an afternoon by eye, or minutes on a commercial index that has keyed the calendar by person. The row stays open and now says what it would cost. || CLOSED 16 September by row 73 rather than by reading the images. If he did not die in England or Wales between 1970 and 1985 — and a 99%-complete index that prints dates of birth says he did not — then there is no English death for an English grant of probate to follow. The 23 unread pages for 1979 would be a search for something now known not to be there. ONE CAVEAT KEPT, because it is real: an English grant CAN follow a foreign death, and the calendar records those in a recognisable form — a page read on the way records ADAMSON, Charles Mary, "of 126 The Gardens Esplanade Durban SOUTH AFRICA died 7 April 1979 administration with will Pietermaritzburg £3500 in England and Wales SEALED London 3 December 1981". So a resealed South African grant would appear. That is a narrower search than the one this row began with, and it is the only reason not to mark the row struck.

rows.what: GRO consular and overseas death registrations for Leonard
rows.note: STRUCK 16 September — not abandoned, but CLOSED STRUCTURALLY, and it is worth more struck than it was open. Row 73 promoted this to the most important untested thing about him. It turns out the series CANNOT CONTAIN HIM, for three separate reasons carrying three different weights. (1) FIRM: the GRO consular death registers run 1849 TO 1965, and both candidate years are outside them. (2) FIRM, from gov.uk itself: the modern statutory service covers deaths "on or after 1 JANUARY 1983" and is optional — 1973 and 1979 are both before it. (3) PROBABLE BUT NOT PROVEN, and marked as such because it is a council web page and not legislation: Coventry City Council's guidance lists SOUTH AFRICA among countries where a death CANNOT be registered with the British authorities at all, alongside Australia, Canada, Bermuda and Zimbabwe — which is what one would expect of Commonwealth countries with their own civil registration. ANY ONE OF THE THREE WOULD BE ENOUGH; ALL THREE AGREE.

rows.what: The GRO death index for England and Wales — in case he went home
rows.note: DONE 16 September, and it is THE BEST-BOUNDED NEGATIVE THIS ARCHIVE HAS EVER PRODUCED ON HIM. Row 58's finding that the family stayed British raised a hypothesis nobody had entertained — that Leonard went home to die. HE DID NOT. FreeBMD transcribes the GRO index; its coverage chart for deaths shows EVERY QUARTER FROM 1970 TO 1983 AT 100%, and the search prints the figure beside each quarter: 58 CONSECUTIVE QUARTERS, EVERY ONE MARKED >99%. And from 1969 the GRO death index carries FULL FORENAMES AND THE DATE OF BIRTH, so he can hide behind neither an initial nor a common surname. Searched WEAR, deaths, March 1970 to December 1985, no forename: 241 ENTRIES, SIXTEEN OF THEM BORN 1915-1919, AND NOT ONE IS HIM. The only 1917 birth is a Sam Wear of Halifax. A separate search on the forename Leonard returns exactly one man, Leonard Rigby Wear born 10 October 1897, died Claro June 1970 — twenty years too old, wrong county. SETTLED: he did not die in England or Wales between 1970 and 1985, in either candidate year or any year between.

rows.what: Sweep every surname in the archive through NAAIRS, now that it can be driven
rows.note: DONE 16 September, and it paid for itself on the fourth surname. THE FIND IS WLD 2225/1953: ILLIQUID CASE. DIVORCE. MORRIS ISAAC SALKOW VERSUS IVONNE (BORN DE FIGUERIDO). THEY MARRIED ON 13 FEBRUARY 1953 AND HE SUED HER FOR DIVORCE IN THE SAME YEAR. The archive knew the marriage ended — FamilySearch has him marrying in 1943, 1953 and 1960 — but not that it ended almost at once; Johannesburg case numbers ran to five figures by the 1970s, so 2225 of 1953 is not a December filing. Three consequences: it removes a stepfather the archive had been assuming was a constant through Derrick's childhood; it explains the hole after 1953 as a fact about her life rather than a failure of searching; and it is a new orderable document naming Ivone, whose summons would recite the date and place of the marriage, both ages and domiciles, and the children by name. ALSO SWEPT: NORQUOY gave Robert Selwyn (row 82); MOMPLE gave the Robertson joint (row 39); CASTLE gave the Longhurst coincidence; SALKOW gave nine Johannesburg estates all inside the index window, one of which is probably Morris Isaac's parent; and LEIBHOLZ returns ZERO across all repositories, which is expected — they were never in South Africa — and is recorded so nobody runs it again.

rows.what: Fill the three null references in the litigation table from NAAIRS itself
rows.note: DONE 15 September. All six rows of litigation.json verified directly against NAAIRS rather than against a commercial mirror or a photograph of somebody's screen. TPD 534/1948 no longer needs its excuse: the index gives it in full — TAB, TPD, VOLUME 5/795, ILLIQUID CASE. DIVORCE. JOHANNES ANTONIE OELOFSE DE WITT VERSUS YVONNE (BORN DE FIGUEIREDO) — and THE VOLUME NUMBER IS NEW, which is what an order form actually needs. The nourl excuse is removed. And WLD 2545/1950 explains its own earlier obscurity: the index spells her IVONE LUWENSKI, not Luwinski, so a correct-spelling surname search could never have found it.

rows.what: The PIO immigration-papers series — Kurt's arrival, and everyone else's
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the answer is that KURT'S ARRIVAL IS NOT IN THE INDEX AT ALL. The PIO immigration series is real and indexed at item level, and it holds exactly one Wear and no Luwinski. KAB PIO 907, reference 38964E, IMMIGRATION PAPERS H C WEAR, 1949 — almost certainly not ours: the initials are H C, not H R or L A R, and 1949 is a decade after this archive dated the family's departure. Recorded because it is the only one and because "almost certainly not" should be written down rather than decided twice. Also found: KAB PIO 82445E, immigration papers re EISENHARDT, 1957. IMMIGRATION+LUWINSKI and PIO+LUWINSKI both return nothing. Kurt has no ship, no permit and no date, and the index that would hold them does not have him.

rows.what: Every WEAR burial at West Park, not just the two this archive stumbled on
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the answer is that LEONARD IS NOT THERE. Searched by collection rather than by guesswork — f.collectionId=4453927, the Johannesburg cemetery registers, 517 raw hits on the surname, collapsed to six distinct people: HENRIETTA WEAR buried 1909, HENRY ROBERT WEAR 13.9.1969, MARTHA MAUD WEAR 19.3.1986, EDWINA ANN WEAR 8.7.2014, MICHELLE ANN WEAR born 1978 died 27.3.2017, and DAN B WEAR undated. He bought grave 56045 and he was not buried in it, and he is in no other Johannesburg cemetery register the collection indexes. BOUNDS: this is the INDEXED layer of ONE collection covering 1840-2019; it does not cover unindexed images in it, other Johannesburg cemeteries, or the Chevrah Kadisha, which is a separate database — a Wear would have no business in a Jewish cemetery but the exclusion is stated rather than assumed. TWO WEARS ARE NEW: Michelle Ann Wear, born 1978, the right age to be a granddaughter of Bruce Wallace Wear who married four times; and Dan B Wear. Both written down, neither pursued.

rows.what: Grave 56045 — is there a stone, and what is carved on it
rows.note: Two people are in that grave and a third person paid sixty pounds for it. A private grave of 1969 in section E.C. would ordinarily carry a memorial, and the burial register has a Remarks column headed "Private Rights, MEMORIALS" in which other rows on the same page record memorials erected and their cost. A photograph of the stone would say who is commemorated and, if a family stone, possibly who paid for it and when it was last added to. Ask the City of Johannesburg cemeteries office, or any of the local volunteer photographers who work West Park. Costs nothing but a request.

rows.what: The undertakers — Cooks in 1969 and REG in 1986
rows.owner: the City of Johannesburg / the firms
rows.note: WORKED 16 September to the limit of what can be established from here, and it is LESS TRACTABLE THAN IT LOOKED. "COOKS" is a specific firm named against Henry Robert Wear in September 1969 and nothing else on that page. "REG", which the 1986 register gives for Martha Maud, IS ALMOST CERTAINLY NOT A FIRM AT ALL — it appears against most rows on the 1969 page as well, which is not how an undertaker's name behaves. It is far likelier to be a clerk's abbreviation, and the archive WILL NOT GUESS WHICH: reading it as a company and writing to that company would be the Caroline Walls error again. Doves, founded 1882 and headquartered in Johannesburg, is the obvious large survivor and could be asked, but there is no evidence connecting it to either entry. WHAT THIS ROW ACTUALLY NEEDS IS THE REGISTER'S OWN KEY — the abbreviation table a cemetery clerk would have used — or one question to the City of Johannesburg cemeteries office, which is the same office row 78 must approach for the photograph of grave 56045. FOLD THE TWO REQUESTS INTO ONE.

rows.what: The five Wear court files, as a set, from the Transvaal depot
rows.note: The archive now knows of five and has read none: WLD 2026/1951 (Phyllis v Leonard, divorce), WLD 790/1957 (Leonard v Norquoy, opposed application), WLD 978/1960 (Kwele v L A R Wear, payment), WLD 2960/1962 (Marjorie v Leonard, divorce) and WLD 2961/1962 (Marjorie v a named woman, damages). A divorce summons of the period recites BOTH PARTIES' FULL NAMES, AGES, DOMICILES AND THE DATE AND PLACE OF THE MARRIAGE, and often the children by name and birth date. Five files from one depot on one visit; the researcher is already holding a brief for the ante-nuptial contracts and this belongs in the same envelope. Supersedes the separate handling of rows 63 and 64. || FOLDED into REQUEST 20 on 16 September — the consolidated Pretoria court-file bundle. Between 15 and 16 September this archive found EIGHT files in one depot, from five separate lines of enquiry, opened as five separate rows. That is how research happens and a terrible way to commission it: one person, one visit, one list, in priority order so it can be cut from the bottom. The bundle is HELD, not sent — the researcher was engaged on 14 September for six Booyzen files and has not replied, and nothing more goes to her until she answers on rates and capacity. This row stays open only as a pointer to request 20.

rows.what: Does a South African marriage register after 1970 have a parents' column?
rows.note: ATTEMPTED 15 September and BLOCKED on image availability, not on reasoning. The test needs a post-1970 South African marriage register image, and the only Wear marriage FamilySearch has indexed with a register image is the WRONG SIDE OF THE LINE: Bruce Wallace Wear and Jillian Anne Thorp, 1959, ark 3:1:3Q9M-CSVT-C992-Q, which this archive already has. His 1977 divorce from Margaret Gannon and his 1980 marriage to Edwina Ann Green are known from GenDatabase and from NAAIRS, NOT from a filmed register, so there is no image to open. The row stays open and now names what it needs: any South African civil marriage register image dated after 1970 — it does not have to be a Wear. The question is about the FORM, not the family, and one page of any post-1970 register would settle whether row 33's finding needs its date range narrowed in public. *** STRUCK 17 SEPTEMBER, AND FOR A REASON WORTH MORE THAN THE ANSWER. *** The row needs any South African civil marriage register image dated after 1970. THERE IS NONE TO REACH BY NAME, because "South Africa, Civil Marriage Records, 1801-1974" IS A NAME INDEX TO 1960, NOT TO 1974. Measured, not assumed: exact-year counts run 133,215 for 1950, 148,400 for 1955, 171,201 for 1959, 178,037 for 1960 - AND THEN 124 FOR 1961, 37 for 1962, 6 for 1966, and nothing at all after 1968. A cliff, not a decline. The 2.69 million images may well run to 1974; the index that lets you find one does not. So this row is not blocked on a sign-in and never was - it is blocked on a boundary inside the collection, and it can only be answered by browsing images or by a register held elsewhere.

rows.what: Phyllis Agnes Robertson — the Norquoy marriage of 14 June 1952, and what became of her
rows.note: ADVANCED 15 September — a candidate name, from NAAIRS. Phyllis remarried a Norquoy on 14 June 1952 and Leonard sued "Phyllis Agnes Norquoy" in 1957. NAAIRS holds fourteen Norquoy documents and two are a Johannesburg man in exactly the right years: WLD 1198/1957, Edward William Allen versus ROBERT SELWYN NORQUOY, and TPD 1624/1960, Sadi Jacobs versus Robert Selwyn Norquoy. ROBERT SELWYN NORQUOY IS VERY PROBABLY HER SECOND HUSBAND — rare Orkney surname, right city, right decade, and WLD 1198/1957 filed the same year as Leonard's WLD 790/1957 against her. Stated as an inference from surname, place and date; no document yet joins them. Next: the 1952 marriage register under the name Norquoy, and his estate. There is no Norquoy estate for a Phyllis Agnes in the index, but the index stops in 1976 and she may have outlived it. || BLOCKED 16 September, and the blocking is specific. She is NOT in the South African death databases under NORQUOY — thirty-one Norquoy records and not a Phyllis among them — so either she died elsewhere, or remarried again, or the index does not have her. The remaining free route is her 1952 marriage register: South African civil marriages are on FamilySearch to 1974, so a June 1952 Johannesburg marriage SHOULD be reachable — but the FamilySearch session has signed out and this archive will not enter credentials. One sign-in unblocks it, together with rows 42, 60, 81 and 88. *** THE NORQUOY FAMILY IS NOW A SHORT LIST INSTEAD OF A SURNAME, 17 September, from the free gazette archive. *** All 41 gazette documents carrying the name were read. IN JOHANNESBURG: THOMAS SMITH LEASK NORQUOY, ambulance officer, estate 3529/44, liquidation account gazetted 1945; SOLDELINA O'NEILL NORQUOY, BORN 14 SEPTEMBER 1900, estate 16050/83, of BRAMLEY HOUSE, 71 LINDEN ROAD, BRAMLEY; LOUIS WILLIAM NORQUOY, a retired miner, estate 1638/55; ROBERT SELWYN NORQUOY; WILLIAM KNIGHT NORQUOY; PETER NORQUOY; BARBARA ALICE NORQUOY; and later Shaun Thomas and Michelle. PHYLLIS MARRIED A NORQUOY ON 14 JUNE 1952 AND ONE OF THESE MEN IS PROBABLY HIM. THIS ARCHIVE IS NOT GOING TO GUESS WHICH — that is exactly how the Giddins mistake was made eight days ago. AND SHE IS NOT IN THE GAZETTE HERSELF: Norquoy AND Phyllis returns nothing; Norquoy AND Agnes returns three documents and all three are coincidental page-mates. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the 1952 marriage register, which names the groom in full — it is already on the researcher's list as part of the Wear court files, and WLD 790/1957 names her as Norquoy, so the summons in that file will carry the surname's owner.

rows.what: Marjorie Eileen Walker, formerly Dunlop — Leonard's second wife
rows.note: DONE 16 September, end to end, and she turns out to be the best-recorded person in Leonard's orbit. MARJORIE EILEEN WALKER, born 1916, died 2003. THREE HUSBANDS AND SIX COURT FILES: WLD 185/1949, divorce, Marjorie Eileen DUNLOP (born Walker) versus Robert John; then 30 October 1951, marries LEONARD at Polana Court, Abel Road, Berea; then WLD 2960/1962 divorcing Leonard and WLD 2961/1962 suing another woman for damages one number later; then WLD 2276/1973 and WLD 7613/1973, Roger William Hannay HUMPHREY against her; then death in 2003 as MARJORIE EILEEN HUMPHREY, BORN WALKER, WITH AN ESTATE FILE. TWO THINGS THIS CHANGES. First, she divorced Dunlop in 1949 and married Leonard in 1951, and Leonard's own divorce is WLD 2026/1951 — two people coming out of two marriages within two years of each other. 1948 sits immediately before her divorce, and the archive's blank nine years for Leonard end exactly where her paper trail begins. Second, and this is the point: SHE WAS MARRIED TO HIM FOR ELEVEN YEARS, THE LONGEST DOCUMENTED RELATIONSHIP OF HIS LIFE, AND HER 2003 ESTATE CARRIES A NEXT-OF-KIN AND HEIRS SCHEDULE THAT LISTS HER CHILDREN.

rows.what: Insolvency and sequestration notices for L. A. R. Wear
rows.note: DONE 15 September, same answer and same reason as row 37. No insolvency or sequestration notice under any exact form of his name, and the loose sweeps are unusable because the surname is an ordinary English word. Recorded as a weak null, explicitly, on the bounded-negatives page.

rows.what: What happened to the Piccadilly Hat Company after 1952
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the shop had a life before Kurt. The 1940 page was unreadable in OCR, so the PDF page was rendered at 200 dpi and read as an image. Government Gazette 2825 of 8 November 1940, page VII: NOTICE OF SALE OF BUSINESS — "The business of PICCADILLY HAT SHOP carried on by PICCADILLY DRESS SALOON (PROPRIETARY), LIMITED, at HANNAH COURT, 81 ELOFF STREET, Johannesburg, has been sold and will be transferred to IVY FUCHS, a public trader, who will carry on the said business under the same style or firm at the same address for her own account and benefit as from the 1st of October, 1940." Attorney Israel Katz, Sauer's Buildings. THREE GAINS: the building is named — HANNAH COURT, which this archive did not have; the shop belonged to a company, PICCADILLY DRESS SALOON (PTY) LTD; and KURT BOUGHT IT FROM A NAMED PREDECESSOR, IVY FUCHS, who had held it for thirteen months. He bought a going concern with a history, not an empty name. Also found: 16 May 1952 no. 4846 lists "Piccadilly Hat Co." in a registration schedule under VCR. 429/8/49, a 1949 registration.

rows.what: Pauline Luwinski's estate — Kurt's widow, died 1985
rows.note: She survived Kurt by seventeen years, was the sequestrating creditor against Phillip Crystal in 1972, traded as Pallou's Dress Centre at 18 Wanderers Street in 1975, and is buried at Westpark, grave V-1470. Her estate is past the NAAIRS cut-off of 1976 and so must be asked for from the Master. Its death notice names HER parents, and its heirs schedule records who was alive in 1985 and what they received — which is the nearest thing to a family list the Luwinski side will ever produce.

rows.what: Read the FamilySearch catalogue at item level, not the browse labels
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the technique transferred but the target did not need it. The catalogue search is /service/search/catalog/v3/search?q.keywords=..., whose replies come back as searchHits[].metadataHit.metadata — not the shape the sister archive's parser expected — and the item call is /service/search/catalog/item/<id>. Applied to Johannesburg it finds olib:4453927, "South Africa, Johannesburg, cemetery registers: COLLECTION RECORD, 1840-2019", and the item record says plainly NOT AVAILABLE ON MICROFILM: it is a digital-image collection, so there is no film_note list of volumes to read and the browse-label problem the technique was invented to solve does not arise here. WHAT REPLACES IT IS BETTER: the collection has an id, and the persona search takes f.collectionId, which turns "every Wear in Johannesburg's cemeteries" into one query. That is how row 77 was answered. NOTE A DISCREPANCY WORTH KNOWING: the item's own summary says the collection holds Olifantsvlei registers 2017-2021 while its title says 1840-2019. The title is right — the 1969 and 1986 West Park entries are in it — so THE SUMMARY IS WRONG, and anyone reading the catalogue description alone would wrongly conclude this collection cannot help them.

rows.what: Run the FamilySearch full-text search over the unindexed South African images
rows.note: Everything this archive has found on FamilySearch has come through the indexed name search or through images it knew to open. FamilySearch now runs full text over images that were never indexed, which is a different instrument: it reads the handwriting on pages nobody catalogued. Run WEAR with LEONARD, LUWINSKI, and MOTA FIGUEIREDO against the South African collections. The cemetery register that broke row 55 open was found by opening images by hand; this is the same act done at scale. || BLOCKED 16 September: THE FAMILYSEARCH SESSION HAS SIGNED OUT and this row cannot move without it. The catalogue and persona APIs now return 401 and the site redirects to the login page. This archive will not enter credentials on David's behalf. One sign-in in the browser unblocks this row, rows 42, 60 and 88 together, and the post-1970 marriage register test in row 81. *** RUN 17 SEPTEMBER, and the answer is a clean negative with a working control. *** The sign-in this row was blocked on is live, and FamilySearch's full-text search — which reads the WORDS ON UNINDEXED IMAGES rather than a name index — answers. LUWINSKI: 26 hits, EVERY ONE AMERICAN — Milwaukee and Chicago naturalisation petitions, New York passenger lists, Ohio and Minnesota vital records. NOT ONE SOUTH AFRICAN. LUWINSKY: four, all American. LUWENSKI: three, all American. 'PICCADILLY HAT', the name of Kurt's own shop at 81 Eloff Street: nothing but Lancashire trade directories. AND THE CONTROL SAYS THE NEGATIVE MEANS SOMETHING, which is the lesson of the Oppenheimer business. Searching NOOITGEDACHT — a farm name that exists almost nowhere else — returns page after page of SOUTH AFRICAN VOTERS' ROLLS 1925-1931, PRETORIA DISTRICT 1927, VEREENIGING 1931 and TRANSVAAL MILITARY RECORDS 1900-1903. SO THE CORPUS REALLY DOES CONTAIN SOUTH AFRICA, and the instrument really was pointed at it. BUT NOW THE LIMIT, STATED PLAINLY: WHAT IT CONTAINS IS 1925-1931 AND 1900-1903. KURT ARRIVED IN 1933. LEONARD SAILED IN 1937. THE WEARS CAME IN 1939. EVERY PERSON THIS ARCHIVE WANTS ARRIVED AFTER THE LAST ROLL WAS PRINTED. The search is exhaustive over the wrong years, which is not the same as exhaustive. IT IS STILL WORTH RE-RUNNING whenever FamilySearch adds South African material, and the four search terms are written down here so that it takes two minutes next time. || ALSO 17 SEPTEMBER: the ordinary index, which is the other half of this row, was worked to completion in row 161.

rows.what: Digitised Johannesburg directories and voters rolls — establish which are reachable from here
rows.note: DONE 16 September, and the answer REDIRECTS THE INSTRUMENT rather than closing it. Row 41 asserted that directories and voters rolls "all need somebody physically in Johannesburg or Pretoria". Checked: FOR THE WEARS THAT IS RIGHT, AND FOR THE OTHER FAMILIES IT IS WRONG. Street directories — the only South African directory digitised and searchable at ancestors.co.za is PIETERMARITZBURG 1897. There is no Johannesburg directory for the 1940s or 1950s reachable without a reading room, so row 41's nine-year hole stays shut from this direction. BUT THE VOTERS ROLLS ARE ONLINE FOR 1925 AND 1931, indexed by town across 148 places including Johannesburg, Berea, Fordsburg, Jeppes, Denver, Langlaagte and Bezuidenhout, through GenDatabase (membership) and eGGSA. 1925 and 1931 are far too early for the Wears, who arrived in the late 1930s — WHICH IS WHY NOBODY HERE HAS USED THEM. But they are exactly right for the families this week has just opened up: the MOMPLES and ROBERTSONS of row 52, who were Johannesburg people by 1950 and whose parents would be on a 1925 or 1931 roll; and the LONGHURSTS of row 91, whose divorces are 1915 and 1919. A roll gives name, address and occupation by street. THAT IS THE CHEAPEST TEST AVAILABLE for whether Maud Mabel Castle's family were in Johannesburg before the Wears came.

rows.what: A register of bounded negatives — what has been searched and did not exist
rows.note: DONE 15 September — /negatives/ is live and in the navigation. Nine bounded negatives, each with three columns: WHAT WAS SEARCHED, WHAT CAME BACK, AND WHAT WOULD STILL FALL OUTSIDE IT. The last column is the point. It holds the distinction between "this is not there", which is a finding, and "I did not find it", which is a shrug. The page also records the two nulls this archive produced by its own error in one evening — a grid read before its async postback had landed, and a form field posted with an empty value — both of which looked exactly like an empty holding and neither of which was. The rule it enforces: do not publish a null you did not bound.

rows.what: Maud Mabel Castle of Johannesburg — coincidence, or the reason the family went there
rows.note: NEW, out of row 39, and deliberately framed as a test rather than a claim. A Maud born Castle was divorcing an Aubrey Leonard Longhurst in Johannesburg in 1915 and again in 1919, two years before Martha Maud Castle bore a son she christened Leonard Aubrey. Martha Maud cannot be that woman — she was nineteen and in Hertfordshire — but a relative could be, and if she was, the archive gains the thing it has never had: A REASON WHY THIS FAMILY CROSSED TO THAT PARTICULAR CITY. Emigrating families go where somebody already is, and the Wear emigration has always been a bare fact with no pull behind it. Three cheap tests, in order: (1) GRO and censuses for a MAUD MABEL CASTLE born in the 1880s in Hertfordshire or Bedfordshire, and whether she sits in the same household or parish as Martha Maud's family at Baldock; (2) MHG 3632/50, Aubrey Leonard Longhurst's estate of 1950, which is INSIDE the estate index's range and orderable, and whose death notice names his parents; (3) WLD 155/1915, whose summons would recite the date and place of the first marriage. If all three come back negative, say so on the bounded-negatives page and close it. || WORKED 16 September to the end of what is free, and test (1) comes back empty. FamilySearch holds NO record anywhere for a MAUD MABEL CASTLE — not in England, not in South Africa, under the full forename pair. A NAAIRS sweep of LONGHURST returns 136 documents and the family is overwhelmingly Cape-based and older — Edwin Richard Percy, Albert, Charles Spurgeon, a customs officer at Port Elizabeth — with nothing joining any of them to a Castle. THAT IS A WEAK NULL and is recorded as one: FamilySearch fuzzy-matches forenames badly and its England coverage is not complete. WHAT IS LEFT IS THE TWO ORDERABLE DOCUMENTS — MHG 3632/50, Aubrey Leonard Longhurst's estate of 1950, inside the index's range; and WLD 155/1915, whose summons would recite the date and place of the marriage. Both need the Pretoria reading room, so this row now belongs with rows 24 and 80 in one visit. || FOLDED into REQUEST 20 on 16 September — the consolidated Pretoria court-file bundle. Between 15 and 16 September this archive found EIGHT files in one depot, from five separate lines of enquiry, opened as five separate rows. That is how research happens and a terrible way to commission it: one person, one visit, one list, in priority order so it can be cut from the bottom. The bundle is HELD, not sent — the researcher was engaged on 14 September for six Booyzen files and has not replied, and nothing more goes to her until she answers on rates and capacity. This row stays open only as a pointer to request 20. It is TIER 3 in that bundle and explicitly the first thing to cut, because it tests a coincidence and not a lead. 17 September: TESTED AGAINST THE ONE SOURCE THAT COULD HAVE PUT A CASTLE IN JOHANNESBURG BEFORE THE FAMILY CAME, and she is not in it. FamilySearch full-text now reaches the SOUTH AFRICAN VOTERS' ROLLS OF 1925-1931. 'Maud Mabel Castle' returns one hit and it is a Washington State birth register; 'Mabel Castle' returns thirty-odd and not one is African. A woman on a voters' roll is an adult British subject resident in the Union, which is exactly what a Castle already in Johannesburg would have been. SHE IS NOT THERE. It does not close the row — she may have arrived after 1931, she may not have registered, and the rolls FamilySearch holds are not all the rolls there were — but the cheapest test has been run and it came back no.

rows.what: Marjorie's estate, 2003 — did she have a son by Leonard, and does he carry the Y
rows.note: NEW, out of row 83, AND IT IS A SECOND LINE ON THE QUESTION ROW 31 HAS BEEN STUCK ON. Marjorie Eileen Humphrey, born Walker, died 2003 with an estate file. An estate's next-of-kin and heirs schedule lists the deceased's children. She was married to Leonard from October 1951 to 1962 — eleven years, the longest documented relationship of his life. IF SHE HAD A SON BY HIM, THAT SON CARRIES LEONARD'S OWN Y CHROMOSOME. Row 31's candidate is Bruce Wallace Wear, Leonard's brother, who if living is NINETY; a son of Leonard born in the 1950s would be in his seventies, and would be a closer test — not the brother's Y but the man's own. Rows 14 and 31 have both been waiting on one ageing man. STATED CAREFULLY: nobody knows whether there were children of that marriage. The archive has never seen a birth, and eleven years without issue is perfectly ordinary. But the schedule is the cheapest place to find out and until now nobody had a reason to look. Her estate is post-1976 so it is at the Master, not in NAAIRS; order it alongside request 19's three sisters.

rows.what: WLD 185/1949 — Marjorie's first divorce, which brackets the blank years
rows.note: NEW, out of row 83, and it belongs in the same Pretoria visit as rows 24, 80 and 91. Marjorie Eileen Dunlop, born Walker, divorced Robert John Dunlop in 1949 and married Leonard in October 1951. A divorce summons of the period recites the date and place of the marriage, the parties' ages and domiciles, AND THE CHILDREN BY NAME AND BIRTH DATE — which is exactly what the estate row wants to know before paying for a copy. It would also place her in Johannesburg in 1949, two years before she married Leonard and one year after 1948. Cheap, because the researcher is already going for five other files. || FOLDED into REQUEST 20 on 16 September — the consolidated Pretoria court-file bundle. Between 15 and 16 September this archive found EIGHT files in one depot, from five separate lines of enquiry, opened as five separate rows. That is how research happens and a terrible way to commission it: one person, one visit, one list, in priority order so it can be cut from the bottom. The bundle is HELD, not sent — the researcher was engaged on 14 September for six Booyzen files and has not replied, and nothing more goes to her until she answers on rates and capacity. This row stays open only as a pointer to request 20.

rows.what: WLD 2225/1953 — the Salkow divorce, filed the year they married
rows.note: NEW, out of row 74's sweep, and it belongs in the Pretoria bundle with rows 24, 80, 91 and 93. WLD 2225/1953, MORRIS ISAAC SALKOW VERSUS IVONNE (BORN DE FIGUERIDO) — the divorce filed the same year as the 13 February 1953 marriage. A divorce summons of the period recites the date and place of the marriage, both parties' ages and domiciles, AND THE CHILDREN BY NAME AND BIRTH DATE. For a woman whose stated age drifts younger on every form she signs, and whose parents are the central unsolved question of this archive, A PLEADING SHE HAD TO ANSWER IS WORTH MORE THAN ANOTHER CERTIFICATE. It may also be the last South African document that records where she was living, which is the thing nobody has been able to establish between 1953 and her death at Porto. || FOLDED into REQUEST 20 on 16 September — the consolidated Pretoria court-file bundle. Between 15 and 16 September this archive found EIGHT files in one depot, from five separate lines of enquiry, opened as five separate rows. That is how research happens and a terrible way to commission it: one person, one visit, one list, in priority order so it can be cut from the bottom. The bundle is HELD, not sent — the researcher was engaged on 14 September for six Booyzen files and has not replied, and nothing more goes to her until she answers on rates and capacity. This row stays open only as a pointer to request 20.

rows.what: GRO marriage certificate — Hitchin, Dec 1939, 3a/4416 — and it names the fathers
rows.note: NEW and URGENT, out of row 62, AND IT IS THE CHEAPEST DOCUMENT ON THE ENTIRE WORK LIST. GRO marriage certificate, HITCHIN, December quarter 1939, VOL 3A PAGE 4416 — Edward J Bailey and Jeanette Eileen Maud Wear. An English marriage certificate names BOTH FATHERS, with their occupations. IF IT NAMES HENRY ROBERT WEAR, this archive has documentary proof from an official record that he had a daughter born 1919 at Hitchin — and the seven-person MyHeritage tree stops being the sole authority for the couple at the head of this line. It does not prove Leonard was their son; nothing yet does. But it is exactly what requests 19 and 20 are trying to achieve the slow and expensive way, for about £14 and an email. BUY THIS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE ON THE LIST, including the GRO birth and marriage certificates of rows 27 and 28.

rows.what: The South African death register at Home Affairs — the only place left
rows.note: NEW, 16 September, AND IT IS NOW THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT ACTION ON THE LIST for the question this archive exists to answer. Four instruments have each looked in a different place and found no death for Leonard Aubrey Robert Wear: the South African estate index (to end 1976), the Johannesburg cemetery registers, the England and Wales death index (1970-1985, >99%, printing dates of birth), and the British consular registers, which structurally cannot hold a South African death of either candidate year. THERE IS EXACTLY ONE PLACE LEFT: THE SOUTH AFRICAN DEATH REGISTER, held by the DEPARTMENT OF HOME AFFAIRS. GenDatabase's 1979 entry is a transcription of that register and is therefore not one source among several but the only source that could exist — and it is flagged INCOMPLETE with the date of birth printed as the corrupt string 0017. WHAT TO ASK FOR: the death register entry (form BI-1663 / the death certificate with full particulars, NOT the abridged version) for WEAR, Leonard Aubrey Robert, died circa 1979. THE FULL CERTIFICATE NAMES THE DECEASED'S PARENTS. So this single document would settle the death year AND test the parentage in one stroke, which nothing else on this list does. BEFORE WRITING: verify the Home Affairs address the way row 48 requires, and check the sent mail — two archives share this mailbox. *** STRENGTHENED 17 SEPTEMBER. *** A fifth and sixth instrument have now looked and cannot reach him: FamilySearch's South African civil death index stops in 1966, and the Transvaal estate-file death notices - which would name his parents - are published for 1955 to 1960 only. The claim that the Home Affairs death register is the ONLY PLACE LEFT now rests on six checks rather than four, and each of them is a bound that was measured rather than a search that came back empty.

rows.what: Answer Ms Xaba — accept her lookup offer, and consolidate to one thread
rows.note: REWRITTEN 16 September after David pointed out that the first draft answered only one of her questions. SHE ASKED THREE THINGS AND THE REPLY NOW ANSWERS ALL THREE IN HER OWN ORDER, IN THE FIRST SIXTY WORDS. (1) "If you would like me to proceed, I can first check TAB, WLD 2545/1950" — YES, PLEASE DO. That is the file in which IVONE IS THE PLAINTIFF, and knowing the grounds and the outcome is worth more than photographs of the others. (2) "Direct your archival enquiries to me directly and keep the correspondence in one thread" — YES, agreed and apologised for. (3) "If you would prefer that the general enquiries address also be copied, I am happy to do so" — NO, SHE ALONE. She offered that for David's convenience; declining removes a step from her day and is the stronger form of the commitment she asked for. THE REPLY ALSO ACKNOWLEDGES THAT SHE ANSWERED HIS OWN QUESTION — court files are bound like the estates — which he had asked twice, at 03:11 and again at 04:11 on 15 September; without acknowledgement she would reasonably wonder whether he read either message. WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO IS HAND HER ANOTHER LIST. She offered to check ONE file — "I can FIRST check" — and this archive has eight more TAB files it would dearly like read. Sending them in the same message as an apology for sending too much would be absurd. Accept the one, and let her come back. ON THE DEAD DOMAIN, the letter says only what is provable: enquiries@dac.gov.za bounced with "the recipient's domain does not exist", and there has been NO REPLY from the others on that domain. IT DOES NOT CLAIM THEY BOUNCED — no NDR for archives@ or naairs@ was ever received, which is odd on the same domain and cannot be explained from here. REVISED AGAIN 16 September. David asked what Ms Xaba actually wants — separate enquiries, or one enquiry listing everything? Her own words settle it: she objects to THE SAME ENQUIRY going to several addresses, not to several enquiries; she writes of "your current ENQUIRIES" in the plural; and she wants them in one thread SO THAT SHE CAN PROVIDE A CONSOLIDATED RESPONSE, which is only possible if she holds the whole picture at once. The draft's promise of "one enquiry at a time, and I will not open another" was an over-correction that would have produced MORE separate replies from her, not fewer. THE LETTER NOW CARRIES THE FULL MANIFEST: all fourteen Transvaal references in two tables, one for the Luwinski/Figueiredo marriage and one for the Wear family, each row with a status — nothing needed, bound and understood, with the researcher, or, for WLD 2545/1950 alone, yes please. It is a manifest, not an order form: no priorities, no fee question, no "please supply", and one sentence above it saying plainly that the only thing being asked of her is 2545/1950. It also tells her the private researcher she recommended is doing eight of them on 22 September, which is the courtesy of showing her that her advice was taken. AMENDED AGAIN 16 September, after David asked whether the letter had been updated for the naturalisation finding. IT HAD NOT, AND IT SHOULD HAVE BEEN. The reason for holding request 24 back was that reply 21 promises 'the only thing I am asking of you is WLD 2545/1950' — but THAT REASONING ONLY APPLIES TO THINGS ADDED AFTER SENDING, AND THE LETTER HAS NOT GONE. Two things changed after it was drafted: the naturalisation angle, and NAAIRS going down. Both now sit in the letter. It tells her NAAIRS has lost its DNS record and returns CICS 400 on every path including its front page — offered as information, not a complaint, because it is NARSSA's own system and she may not have been told; it is the only thing in the letter that is a gift rather than an ask. And it asks ONE question that needs no file pulled: is there an index entry under FIGUEIREDO or MOTA FIGUEIREDO in the naturalisation or alien-registration series at SAB. The promise sentence was amended from 'the only thing I am asking of you' to 'THE ONLY FILE I AM ASKING FOR' so that it stays literally true. The question carries its own off-ramp — 'if the answer is simply nothing under that surname, that is a genuinely useful answer and I will stop looking down that road' — and it points her at the father rather than the daughter, with the reason, so she is not sent hunting for a file the law of the day may have made unnecessary. EVERYTHING ELSE IN REQUEST 24 STAYS HELD. READ END TO END 16 September before sending, and TWO THINGS WERE WRONG. (1) THE NATURALISATION PARAGRAPH WAS GARBLED — an earlier edit had spliced two versions and left 'And it is more likely to be her father than her' stranded AFTER the closing sentence, so the paragraph ended mid-argument. Rewritten. (2) IT STILL SAID 'from what I can see on NAAIRS', which the Oppenheimer control had overtaken by then. It now tells her plainly that the online index does not list naturalisation files at all — with the proof, a man whose application is printed in the Gazette of 20 February 1942 and whose file is not indexed — which turns a vague request into a specific reason for asking HER rather than looking himself. ALSO REFORMATTED FOR EMAIL: the markdown pipe tables would have arrived as pipes and dashes in Outlook, and the backticks round dac.gov.za would have printed literally. Plain-text send version at requests/21-SEND-THIS-to-mavis.txt. *** SENT 16 SEPTEMBER 2026, message 1a0a9d94c42e1756, inside thread 1a0a30c59c9c8405. Sent to her ALONE, not reply-all — she had copied Enquiries2 on her own message, and a letter that declines the cc should not arrive carrying one. ***

rows.what: Answer Anne — confirm the six, and ask by when the extra files must be listed
rows.note: DRAFTED as REPLY 22, not sent, AND IT IS TIME-CRITICAL. She replied on 15 September with a quote and a date: R2,850 for the first file INCLUDING THE DRIVE TO PRETORIA, then subsequent files charged by the work in them, "not to exceed R2,000" each — the sentence is garbled and the ceiling should be confirmed rather than assumed. No per-page or hourly charge. Invoice before the visit. She confirms MHG 52653 is a normal reference despite the missing year. AND SHE OFFERS TUESDAY 22 SEPTEMBER. HER COST STRUCTURE IS THE WHOLE ARGUMENT: the first file carries the journey and every later file is cheap BECAUSE SHE IS THERE ANYWAY. Request 20 holds eight more TAB files and the Lerena archive has at least five. EVERY FILE ADDED TO THIS TRIP IS CHEAP; EVERY FILE THAT MISSES IT COSTS ANOTHER R2,850. The list is not ready, so the reply confirms the six, accepts the date, and asks one question: by when does she need the additional references to include them on the 22nd. REWRITTEN ENTIRELY 16 September after David asked whether the Anne and Mavis letters were up to date. MAVIS'S WAS. ANNE'S WAS NOT — its central premise had been overtaken by two emails nobody had read. HER TERMS, 15 Sep 20:02: NO per page, NO hourly, NO call-out; R2,850 FOR THE FIRST FILE including the drive to Pretoria and back; each file after that charged by how much work it took, NOT TO EXCEED R2,000; 'I would not exploit the situation in any way.' She capped her own downside unprompted. INVOICE FIRST, THEN SHE TRAVELS. HER MESSAGE OF 16 Sep 08:46: the invoice is coming, it covers THE SIX MHG FILES PLUS A SEVENTH FREE — MHG 10245/69, the Wear death notice, 'as I can see it is just one page, so I am giving it to you for nothing' — and SHE GOES ON TUESDAY 22 SEPTEMBER IF THE INVOICE IS ACCEPTED. THE OLD DRAFT'S 'SCALE PROBLEM' IS DEAD. It agonised over 26 items against 6 quoted; she has settled the scope herself — 'So lets do the 6, and it will go well' — and has ALREADY AGREED IN PRINCIPLE to the CJC Marico files, the OD series and the Bloemfontein estates: 'I can do this for you.' Raising a scale problem now would solve a problem she has already solved. The tiered appendix is HELD for the second visit. AND SHE ASKED ONE DIRECT QUESTION WHICH IS THE ONLY THING HOLDING HER UP: 'For the ANC at the deeds office, we need the name and the date. (you did give me the dates,)' SHE IS RIGHT AND IT IS THIS ARCHIVE'S OMISSION — the 03:25 email of 15 September gave her two dates and NAMED NOBODY, and a deeds registry indexes ante-nuptial contracts by the parties. The reply supplies all three with names: 19 JUNE 1948, KURT ISRAEL LUWINSKI and IVONE born MOTA FIGUEIREDO formerly DE WITT; 29 FEBRUARY 1956, register entry No. 169, KURT ISRAEL LUWINSKI and FRANCES HOSTOWSKY; and 30 OCTOBER 1951, certificate 1397, LEONARD AUBREY ROBERT WEAR and MARJORIE EILEEN DUNLOP born WALKER — THE THIRD IS NEW TO HER AND IS THE ONE TO GET, because it is the only one that names Leonard and an ANC recites each party's full particulars rather than a register's eleven columns. DAVID'S ACTIONS IN ORDER: wait for the invoice and pay it, because she does not travel until it is settled and Tuesday is six days off; send the reply so the names reach her first; do NOT send the appendix. REFORMATTED FOR EMAIL 16 September. The three group tables were markdown pipe tables and would have arrived in Outlook as a wall of pipes and dashes — for a woman about to work from them at a reading-room desk, that is not a cosmetic problem. Rewritten as indented numbered items with the reference on one line and the want beneath it, which also survives printing. Plain-text send version at requests/22-SEND-THIS-to-anne.txt. *** SENT 16 SEPTEMBER 2026, message 1a0a9d8a6c8c5783, inside her existing thread 1a0a234a65602bca. *** WHAT IS NOW OUTSTANDING IS DAVID'S, NOT THE ARCHIVE'S: she does not travel until the invoice is settled and Tuesday is six days off. AND A CONSEQUENCE TO EXPECT — the letter widens the job from seven items to twenty-six and explicitly invites a revised invoice, so a larger number may come back before Tuesday. That is the price of one drive instead of two and it was taken deliberately.

rows.what: CORRECTED: four living DNA match holders were named on the published site
rows.note: FOUND AND FIXED 16 September, and it is the most serious error this archive has made. The standing rule is that LIVING DNA MATCH HOLDERS ARE NEVER NAMED — role, country and cM only. They never consented to anything and their names reached this archive solely because they share chromosomes with Derrick. FOUR WERE PUBLISHED IN FULL on /worklist/ and FIVE MORE BY SURNAME on /dna/, in a sentence identifying them as people rather than as ancestral surnames. It was found only because the AutoClusters export arrived and gave, for the first time, an authoritative list of all 111 match holders to check the build against. NOTHING CAUGHT IT BECAUSE NOTHING WAS LOOKING: check-living guards the people in the family REGISTER and says "none present" while four match holders sat on the work-list page. Both pages are corrected and rebuilt. THE DURABLE FIX IS tools/check-matches.py, now wired as npm run check:matches: it cross-references every name in the export against every built page, flags full names always and surnames unless they are on a documented AMBIGUOUS list — Halsey and Morris and Brown are there because they are also DEAD people in this archive, with the reason written beside each. It degrades gracefully: with no export on the machine it SKIPS and says so, rather than giving a false all-clear. Verified by injecting a name into the build and confirming it fails.

rows.what: Test the 165.9 cM match against the twelve-region Wear signature
rows.note: NEW, out of the AutoClusters report, AND IT OUTRANKS ROW 44's CANDIDATE. Cluster 3 — the paternal cluster — holds twelve people and 1,706 cM, nearly a third of all clustered sharing in the kit. Eight of the twelve HAVE NEVER APPEARED IN THIS ARCHIVE, and one of them shares 165.9 cM, WHICH MAKES HIM THE FOURTH-LARGEST MATCH DERRICK HAS. At that level he is closer than a second cousin. Run his segments against data/wear-signature.json: if most fall in the twelve regions the Castle cousins do not share, the Wear line has a second living witness and row 31's Y-DNA problem gains another candidate to approach. Needs the chromosome browser, so it needs the sign-in. DO NOT NAME HIM ANYWHERE IN THE SITE.

rows.what: Write to the Portuguese matches about Ivone's parents
rows.note: DRAFTED as REQUEST 23, HELD — these go to living private individuals and only David can send them, which row 6 already establishes. THE CASE FOR THEM IS THE STRONGEST THING IN THE AUTOCLUSTERS REPORT. Four of the twenty clusters are Portuguese — fifteen people, about 776 cM — and because Derrick's mother was Portuguese from Lourenço Marques, EVERY ONE OF THEM IS ON HER SIDE. Three separate clusters means three separate ancestral couples, which is what a Figueiredo–Mota marriage plus their own parents' lines should look like; one is probably the MOTA line and another the FIGUEIREDO. THE SCALE, PLAINLY: the strongest shares 133.2 cM, MORE THAN ANYONE THIS ARCHIVE HAS EVER WRITTEN TO ABOUT IVONE, and more than the letters to Lisbon, Maputo and Porto have produced between them. The letters are in Portuguese with English below, sent through MyHeritage's own messaging because the export gives tree links and not addresses. ONE MESSAGE PER CLUSTER, to the strongest member, saying openly that one or two others in the same group are being written to — NOT all fifteen, who may well know each other and would read fifteen near-identical messages as harvesting. Order: the 133.2 cM cluster, then the one with two over 100, then the one whose members share an 8,911-person tree, then the weakest only if the others produce nothing. WHAT IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT: anything about the paternity question. It is Derrick's private business, it concerns his FATHER's side, and it has no bearing on what a Portuguese cousin can help with. The maternal line is not in doubt, and a stranger told a delicate thing in a first message usually stops replying. The ask is one question — do the names MOTA, FIGUEIREDO or PINTO DA ROCHA appear in your family, and is there any link to Mozambique — with an explicit statement that no money or estate is involved. THE FIRST USEFUL ANSWER IS A PLACE: a parish or district in Portugal. With a parish the Portuguese civil registers become searchable and row 65's dead end reopens at no cost.

rows.what: The Xaba queue — the questions whose answer is a sentence, not a photograph
rows.note: RAISED 16 September, when David asked whether anything from the Booyzen and Lerena sessions ought to go to Ms Xaba rather than to Anne. CHECKING THE ASSIGNMENT SHOWED ALL 26 ITEMS POINTED AT ANNE, AGAINST A SIX-ITEM BOOKING — and several of them are the wrong shape for a paid research day. THE THING THAT CHANGED IS BIGGER THAN THE LIST: since 14 September this archive has read "we are unable to SCAN these files" as "bound files are unreachable". She never said she could not READ them, and her offer on WLD 2545/1950 proves she will look at a file and say what it is in. A J294 death notice is wanted for one thing — who does it name as parents, spouse, children — and that is a sentence. This archive has been commissioning photographs of sentences. THE QUEUE IS RANKED BY HOW BADLY AN ITEM SUITS A RESEARCHER. Q1: the two doubtful references, TAB MHG O/2899 and MHG 52653, which Anne is being told to skip — a bad reference is a desk question, and Ms Xaba has already demonstrated exactly that skill by finding WLD 2545/1950 where NAAIRS spells the surname Luwenski. Q2: whether the OD correspondence-register numbers pull as discrete items or sit inside bound volumes — one sentence from her decides whether Anne spends ten minutes or ninety. Q3: CJC vol 907 ref 104 and SAB VWR 2 B645/8/38, where the index line is the entire catalogue record. Q4: four death notices, held back deliberately because a photograph beats a summary and Anne is already going — they are the fallback if her day runs out, so that the answer is a question rather than a second invoice. NOTHING GOES UNTIL SHE ANSWERS ON 2545/1950. Reply 21 told her the only thing being asked of her was that file, and breaking it in the next message would cost more than the whole queue is worth. When it does go, Q1 and Q2 travel together in one message — they are all 'does this exist and how does it pull' — which is the consolidation reply 21 promised.

rows.what: Ivone's alien file — or her father's, which would name every child
rows.note: RAISED 16 September, from David's question: a woman naturalised out of Lourenço Marques would have a file naming her parents, wouldn't she? THE RECORD CLASS IS REAL AND THIS ARCHIVE HAS NEVER TESTED IT. A South African naturalisation memorial asks for date and place of birth, THE FATHER'S NAME AND NATIONALITY, the date and ship of arrival, and the wife and children by name and age. AND THE FATHER'S FILE WOULD BE BETTER THAN HERS — it names every child, so it would give her parents AND her siblings in one document, which nothing this archive has tried can do. BUT THE LAW MAY HAVE REMOVED HER OWN FILE BEFORE IT EXISTED. An alien woman who married a British subject before 2 September 1949 acquired his nationality automatically; the South African Citizenship Act 44 of 1949 ended that and required an alien wife to naturalise like a man. IVONE MARRIED JOHANNES ANTONIE OELOFSE DE WITT ON 2 FEBRUARY 1948, nineteen months inside the old rule. If de Witt was a Union national she became one by marriage and there is no file for her — AND NATIONALITY ACQUIRED BY MARRIAGE SURVIVED THE DIVORCE, so TPD 534/1948 does not undo it. THAT MAKES DE WITT'S OWN NATIONALITY A QUESTION WORTH ANSWERING, because it decides whether her file can exist. THE GAZETTE HAS ALREADY BEEN SWEPT: 1930 to 1960, every year, surname Figueiredo, South African issues only — no naturalisation notice, with the control test run first and passing. On /negatives/. NAAIRS, which indexes the SAB naturalisation files, WAS UNREACHABLE on the day. The enquiry is queued for Ms Xaba as Q5 of request 24, framed as 'is there an index entry for the surname' rather than 'find her file'.

rows.what: Two Figueiredo estates found in the gazette — one of them from Lourenço Marques
rows.note: FOUND 16 September as a by-product of the naturalisation sweep, and neither was known to this archive. ESTATE 7029/54 — FIGUEIREDO, AGOSTINHO VICENTE SEBASTIAO, of Johannesburg, first and final account advertised 22 July 1955. ESTATE 2910/60 — MONTEIRO, JOSÉ DE FIGUEIREDO, OF LOURENÇO MARQUES, PORTUGUESE EAST AFRICA, executor Frederick William Damant c/o Standard Bank, advertised 2 December 1960. THE SECOND IS THE INTERESTING ONE: a man of Lourenço Marques whose estate was administered in the Union, in the decade after Ivone's marriages, which is exactly the profile of somebody the family might have known or been. NEITHER IS CLAIMED AS A RELATIVE — Figueiredo is a common Portuguese surname and 'Monteiro, José de Figueiredo' is a different name from hers. What makes them worth a row is that each has an estate number, and a South African estate file holds a death notice, form J294, which asks for the deceased's parents. THE CHEAP NEXT STEP IS THE GAZETTE, NOT THE FILE: an estate is advertised more than once, and the earlier notices carry the date of death and often the address.

rows.what: The six spellings of her name — write them down once, and put them in front of anyone searching
rows.note: RAISED 16 September on David's suggestion, and it is the kind of thing that decides whether a search works. IVONE IS RECORDED UNDER SIX SPELLINGS OF HER MAIDEN SURNAME ACROSS FIVE DOCUMENTS, and NAAIRS itself carries two of the worst. FORENAME: IVONE in most files, YVONNE in TPD 534/1948, IVONNE in WLD 2225/1953. MAIDEN SURNAME: FIGUEIREDO and DE FIGUEIREDO; MOTA FIGUEIREDO in WLD 1950/1948; DE FIGUERIDO in WLD 2225/1953; DE FIGUEREDO on her own 1953 marriage register; and FIGARETTO in the NAAIRS index. MARRIED SURNAMES: DE WITT from February 1948, LUWINSKI — also LUWINSKY and LUWENSKI — from June 1948, SALKOW from February 1953. THE PROOF THAT IT MATTERS IS THE FILE MS XABA HAS OFFERED TO CHECK: WLD 2545/1950 hid from this archive for weeks because the index spells her LUWENSKI. The table now goes into reply 21, framed as saving her a search rather than instructing her. IT ALSO COST THIS ARCHIVE A NEGATIVE: the gazette naturalisation sweep had searched only three of the six spellings. RE-RUN THE SAME DAY across all six plus the married names — no naturalisation notice under any of them, and FIGARETTO, FIGUEIRIDO and LUWENSKI turn out to appear NOWHERE IN ANY AFRICAN GAZETTE, which makes them index corruptions rather than spellings anyone ever printed. The negative on /negatives/ is corrected and is now stronger than when it was first written, not weaker.

rows.what: The names page — every spelling she is filed under, on the site rather than in a commit message
rows.note: DONE 16 September on David's instruction: 'can you also make sure the site is clear on the different spellings'. NEW PAGE /names/, in the primary nav after Ivone, with data in site/src/data/names.json. FOURTEEN FORMS, each given with the record it comes from and marked as either a document variant or an index corruption — a distinction that matters, because an index corruption tells you about the cataloguer and a document variant tells you about the family. Three forenames: IVONE, YVONNE (TPD 534/1948), IVONNE (WLD 2225/1953).
